design_detail: Randomized, saline-controlled, within-person laboratory study in healthy volunteers at Yale and the West Haven Veterans Affairs Medical Center. Each participant had three test days in random order: a 40-minute constant intravenous infusion of saline, of ketamine hydrochloride 0.1 mg/kg or of ketamine hydrochloride 0.5 mg/kg. The abstract calls the study double-blind; the Methods do not describe how the infusions were masked or whether raters knew the condition, and no blinding check is reported. Ratings were made 30 and 15 minutes before the infusion, 10 minutes into it, and 40, 70 and 190 minutes after it ended (the 80-, 110- and 230-minute time points); the frontal tests (continuous performance test, Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, letter fluency) were given between 20 and 40 minutes, that is during the infusion; three-word recall was tested before the infusion and at 10, 80, 110 and 230 minutes. Measures: BPRS key positive and negative symptom items and two BPRS factors, the Clinician-Administered Dissociative States Scale (CADSS), the self-rated Perceptual Aberration Scale, the MMSE, clinician-rated visual analogue mood scales, plasma cortisol, prolactin, HVA and MHPG, blood pressure and pulse. The card-sorting test was analysed between participants on their first test day only. Ketamine blood levels were not measured; plasma levels were predicted from published pharmacokinetic parameters. No patients were studied, and the interval between test days is not stated.
can_establish: Whether single 40-minute intravenous infusions of ketamine at two subanaesthetic doses, compared with saline in the same people, change clinician-rated and self-rated psychotic-like and dissociative symptoms, simple cognitive test scores, mood ratings, hormones and blood pressure during and shortly after the infusion in 18 screened healthy volunteers.
cannot_establish: Anything about effects beyond the test day (follow-up was an unstructured interview the next day and at later test days), about repeated or non-medical use, other routes, or people with psychiatric or substance-use histories; the plasma concentrations that produced the effects (none were measured); and, because recall was tested with three-word sets that stayed near the maximum and card sorting was compared between 5 to 8 people per dose on their first day, whether immediate recall is really spared or how large the card-sorting effect is.

sample.recruitment: Public advertisement in the community; participants were paid (p. 200).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Two-step screen: a structured psychiatric interview excluding any psychiatric disorder or substance use disorder (the paper's DSM-III-R wording is substance abuse disorders), any past consultation for an emotional difficulty, psychiatric illness in a first-degree relative, or significant current life stress (3 or more on the DSM-III-R Axis IV Severity of Psychosocial Stressors Scale); then a telephone interview with an informant named by the participant, at which nobody was excluded. No psychoactive medication for the 4 weeks before testing, supported by urine toxicology at screening and on test days; no serious medical illness, normal physical examination and laboratory tests including liver and thyroid function; scores within normal limits on the Bell Reality Testing Inventory and the Wisconsin Scales of Psychosis Proneness (p. 200).
sample.demographics: As printed: 12 men (mean age 23.7 years, SEM 0.9; mean weight 79.4 kg, SEM 3.2) and 7 women (mean age 25.9 years, SEM 0.9; mean weight 65.9 kg, SEM 4.7). Because one man dropped out, the 18 completers were presumably 11 men and 7 women (see reporting issues). Ethnicity, education and previous experience of ketamine or other drugs are not reported (p. 200).
sample.attrition: One man dropped out after his first test day, on which he had received 0.5 mg/kg; no reason is given (p. 200). His first-day card-sorting data are in the 19-person card-sorting analysis (p. 206). The analysed number varies by measure: 18 for the BPRS scores, Perceptual Aberration Scale, MMSE, mood scales, prolactin and blood pressure; 17 for the CADSS; 16 for recall and cortisol; 15 for verbal fluency (three excluded because they had not finished the test before the infusion ended, p. 201) and MHPG; 14 for the continuous performance test (introduced after four participants had entered, p. 201) and HVA. Reasons are given only for the continuous performance test and verbal fluency (pp. 201-208).
sample.selection_effects: Young, paid community volunteers screened to exclude any personal or family psychiatric history, substance use disorder, recent stress and high psychosis-proneness: a sample selected for low risk, which the authors suggest may be why the pre-test psychosis-proneness measures did not predict the symptom response (p. 211). Previous drug experience is not reported. The results describe screened healthy volunteers in a hospital research unit and cannot be carried over to people who use ketamine non-medically, to people with psychiatric histories or to patients.

exposure.measurement: Drug given by the investigators (ketamine hydrochloride, Parke-Davis; saline as placebo). Ketamine blood levels were not measured: published pharmacokinetic parameters were fitted into constant-infusion equations to predict plasma levels of 0.025 to 0.05 mg/L during the 0.1 mg/kg condition and 0.1 to 0.25 mg/L during the 0.5 mg/kg condition (p. 200). Abstinence from psychoactive medication was supported by urine toxicology at screening and on test days.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as the investigators gave them: single intravenous infusions over 40 minutes of saline, of ketamine hydrochloride 0.1 mg/kg (0.0025 mg/kg per minute) or of ketamine hydrochloride 0.5 mg/kg (0.0125 mg/kg per minute), one condition per test day, three test days in random order; doses are expressed as the hydrochloride salt. The paper says the two doses were chosen from pilot data and published reports as behaviourally active but subanaesthetic. Before each test day the possible responses were reviewed with the participant (p. 200). The interval between test days is not stated; the text mentions interviews in subsequent weeks (p. 201).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported beyond the exclusion of substance use disorders and the 4-week abstinence from psychoactive medication with urine screens; alcohol, tobacco, caffeine and illicit drug use are not described (p. 200).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: No psychoactive medication for 4 weeks, supported by urine toxicology at screening and on each test day (p. 200).

comparison.controls: Each participant's own saline test day (within-person placebo). The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test cannot be repeated, so it was compared between participants on their first test day only: 6 had placebo, 5 had 0.1 mg/kg and 8 had 0.5 mg/kg (pp. 200-201, 206).
comparison.matching: Within-person comparison; the order of the three test days was randomized (method and allocation concealment not described). Changes from baseline on ketamine days were also corrected by subtracting the placebo-day change at the same time point (p. 201).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the within-person comparisons. For the between-participant card-sorting comparison no baseline cognitive measure and no comparison of the three first-day groups is reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (the same people served as their own controls).

outcomes.instruments: Clinician-rated: Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS), with four key positive items (conceptual disorganization, hallucinatory behavior, suspiciousness, unusual thought content), three key negative items (blunted affect, emotional withdrawal, motor retardation) and the activation and hostility-suspiciousness factors; the Clinician-Administered Dissociative States Scale (CADSS), a measure of perceptual, behavioural and attentional alterations during dissociation, 19 self-report questions and 8 observer ratings scored 0 to 4, split by the authors on face validity into five subscales (body perception, environmental perception, feelings of unreality, memory impairment, time perception); 100-mm visual analogue scales for anger, anxiety, drowsiness, high and sadness, marked by the clinician according to what the participant reported and showed. Self-rated: Perceptual Aberration Subscale of the Wisconsin Psychosis Proneness Scale (perceptual changes of the kind reported in schizophrenia). Cognitive: Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE, global cognition) with an added 10-minute delayed recall, a new three-word set at each time point recalled immediately, after a distracting task and after 10 minutes; a continuous performance test of vigilance (press a button when a 9 follows a 1); letter fluency (words beginning with a given letter in 1 minute, parallel letters across days); a computerized Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (rule learning and set shifting; an unpublished in-house version). Biochemical: plasma prolactin and cortisol by radioimmunoassay, free homovanillic acid (HVA, a dopamine metabolite) and 3-methoxy-4-hydroxyphenethyleneglycol (MHPG, a noradrenaline metabolite) by gas chromatography and mass spectrometry. Physiological: blood pressure and pulse (pp. 200-201).
outcomes.validity_norms: The BPRS, the CADSS (validated in healthy people and in post-traumatic stress disorder), the Perceptual Aberration Scale, the MMSE and letter fluency are established instruments; the five CADSS subscales and the computerized card-sorting version are not validated as used, and no norms are applied to any score. The recall task is very easy: immediate recall stays near the maximum of 3 words on every day (Figure 4, p. 207) and the authors themselves call it a simple test of learning three words (p. 210). The continuous performance test was near its ceiling on placebo (29.7 of 30 targets, p. 205).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Impairment' is a significant fall from baseline, or from the placebo-day change at the same time point, by Dunnett's tests after a significant dose x time interaction; 'positive' and 'negative symptoms' are the sums of the selected BPRS items. Timing: the 10-minute ratings and all the frontal tests fell during the infusion; the 80-minute ratings were made 40 minutes after the infusion ended but covered the period since the previous rating, which the authors say reflects the last 30 minutes of the infusion (p. 200). Everything reported is a short-lived effect within the test day in healthy volunteers; the only later checks were an unstructured interview the next day and at later test days (pp. 201, 209).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Within each measure Dunnett's tests control the comparisons with baseline and with placebo, but there is no correction across measures. Editors' count of 39 outcome measures analysed: 4 BPRS scores, CADSS total and 5 subscales, Perceptual Aberration Scale, MMSE, 4 continuous performance measures, verbal fluency, 7 card-sorting measures, 3 recall conditions, 5 mood scales, 4 biochemical measures and 3 cardiovascular measures; the 7 individual BPRS items were also analysed separately, and the correlation analyses are additional (pp. 201-209).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not described. 'Double-blind' appears in the abstract (p. 199) and nowhere in the Methods, which give the randomized order but not how the infusions were masked, who made the ratings, or whether the rater knew the condition; no blinding check is reported. Participants were told before each test day what responses to expect (p. 200). On the 0.5 mg/kg day 8 of 18 had blurred vision, about half of them with nystagmus, and 2 vomited (p. 209), so that condition would have been evident to participants and raters.

analysis.effect_sizes: The paper gives ANOVA F tests, Dunnett's t values and, for the cognitive, peak-mood, biochemical and cardiovascular measures, means with SEM; no confidence intervals and no standardized effect sizes. Within-person dose x time interactions: BPRS four key positive symptoms F8,136=22.9, three key negative symptoms F8,136=18.0, CADSS total F6,96=46.0, Perceptual Aberration Scale F6,102=20.0 (all P=.0001), 10-minute delayed recall F8,120=3.4 (P=.002) (pp. 203-207). Verbal fluency 16.1 (SEM 1.3), 15.1 (1.2) and 12.9 (1.3) words for placebo, 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg, the high dose against placebo F1=8.4, P=.007 (p. 206); editors' calculation: a within-person standardized difference of about 0.75 (square root of 8.4, divided by the square root of 15). Card sorting between first-day groups: perseverative errors 6.5 (SEM 0.8, n=6), 16.8 (7.9, n=5) and 31.9 (7.0, n=8) (p. 206); editors' calculation: SDs of about 2.0, 17.7 and 19.8, so the 0.5 mg/kg against placebo difference is about 1.7 pooled SDs (Hedges' g about 1.6), on very unequal spread. Placebo-corrected peak blood-pressure rise at 0.5 mg/kg about 7.3 mm Hg systolic (18.6 minus 11.3) and 6.6 mm Hg diastolic (12.5 minus 5.9), editors' calculation from peak changes that are not time-matched (p. 209).
analysis.covariates: None for most outcomes. Where test-day baselines differed the baseline was used as a covariate: for HVA, the baseline on the 0.5 mg/kg day was 10.3 against 14.7 ng/mL on placebo, and after covariance the dose effect was no longer significant (F2,25=0.9, P=.4) while the dose x time interaction remained (pp. 201, 208). Sex was not analysed; the authors state only that it did not appear to influence responses and that data were collapsed across sexes (p. 200). Order, period and carryover effects are not modelled.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or pre-specified primary outcome is mentioned; the paper predates trial registration.
analysis.selective_reporting: The three recall conditions, the five mood scales and the four biochemical measures are reported in full, including null results, which lowers the concern. But the measures are reported as F and t statistics and figures rather than tables, no table of means exists for the symptom scales, and several analyses appear only when they are significant: the peak-change ANOVA for drowsiness is reported because it was significant after a non-significant overall analysis (p. 207), and the 'placebo-corrected peak increase' used for the psychosis-proneness correlations is not defined among the planned measures. The CADSS subscale item lists were available from the authors on request and are not printed (p. 201).
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. The symptom effects are large and consistent, but the secondary analyses are small: the card-sorting comparison rests on 6, 5 and 8 people, and the correlations within the first test day (n=19) or within the ketamine day (n=16 to 18) are very imprecise. Editors' calculation: with n=15 to 19 the study has roughly 19% power to detect a true correlation of 0.3 at P=.05 two-sided, so the null correlations between memory impairment and symptom scores cannot show that the two are unrelated.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 18 screened healthy volunteers, a 40-minute intravenous infusion of ketamine 0.5 mg/kg raised BPRS positive and negative symptom scores, dissociative and perceptual-alteration scores, reduced the number of words produced in a fluency test and the number of words recalled after a 10-minute delay, produced more perseverative errors in card sorting (a between-participant comparison of 6, 5 and 8 people on their first day), left global cognition on the MMSE and immediate three-word recall unchanged, raised plasma cortisol and prolactin, blunted the day's fall in HVA, did not change MHPG, and raised blood pressure modestly. Scores returned to baseline generally within about 15 minutes after the infusion ended. The 0.1 mg/kg condition produced few significant changes: a rise in negative symptoms at the 80-minute time point and a fall in anxiety that was not significant once the placebo-day fall was taken into account.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports that ketamine impaired performance on vigilance, verbal fluency and the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test and preferentially disrupted delayed word recall, sparing immediate and postdistraction recall (p. 199). The first claim is supported only for the high dose, and for card sorting it rests on a between-participant comparison of 6, 5 and 8 people on their first test day, which is not stated in the abstract. The claim that immediate recall was spared rests on a task at which participants recalled close to all three words on every day, so the comparison is between a ceiling-level task and one with room to fall; the Discussion concedes this, noting that a 24-word task in another study did show an immediate-recall effect and that attention, consolidation and retrieval cannot be separated (pp. 210-211). The Conclusions say the data indicate that NMDA antagonists produce a broad range of symptoms, behaviors and cognitive deficits resembling aspects of endogenous psychoses (p. 199); the Comment is more careful, stating that the state is not identical to schizophrenia or to dissociative states (p. 211). The statement that subanaesthetic doses may be given to healthy volunteers in controlled laboratory settings without significant risk of untoward psychological consequences (p. 209) rests on 18 heavily screened people followed up by unstructured interview, which cannot support a safety conclusion. Describing the study as double-blind in the abstract goes beyond the Methods, which describe no masking procedure.

timeline.event: A placebo-controlled within-person infusion study in 15 healthy volunteers reported lower free recall and recognition memory and raised BPRS thought-disorder and withdrawal-retardation scores during the infusion, and argued that the memory effect was not secondary to attention or to the symptom ratings

A four-condition steady-state infusion study in 15 healthy men reproduced the dose-dependent rise in positive and negative symptom scores and the fall in declarative memory, with measured plasma concentrations, and found no effect on vigilance, fluency or spatial working memory at those concentrations
Positron emission tomography studies of (S)- and (R)-ketamine in healthy volunteers, to be appraised from their full texts, report the psychopathological profile with regional brain metabolism
An infusion study in people with schizophrenia reported a brief return of their own symptoms, extending the model from healthy volunteers to patients (to be appraised from the full text)

replication.where_it_stands: The acute, short-lived increase in psychotic-like and dissociative ratings and the fall in delayed verbal recall during subanaesthetic intravenous ketamine in healthy volunteers have been reproduced repeatedly, including with measured plasma concentrations (Newcomer et al., 1999). What has not held up uniformly is the pattern across cognitive domains: this study found effects on vigilance, fluency and card sorting at 0.5 mg/kg given over 40 minutes, whereas the steady-state study of Newcomer et al. (1999) found declarative memory affected and vigilance, fluency and spatial working memory not affected, which the later authors attribute to the different infusion conditions and plasma concentrations. Whether immediate recall is spared is unresolved and depends on task difficulty.

funding.funder: As printed (p. 212): funding from the Department of Veterans Affairs through the Schizophrenia Biological Research Center and the Department of Veterans Affairs-Yale Alcoholism Research Center, West Haven, Connecticut, and a Merit Review Grant from the Department of Veterans Affairs (Dr Krystal); additional funding from research grant MH-30929 from the National Institute of Mental Health, Bethesda, Maryland.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the paper carries no conflict-of-interest statement, which was not usual practice in 1994.
funding.affiliations_note: Academic and Veterans Affairs psychiatry departments (Yale University School of Medicine, West Haven VA Medical Center, Connecticut Mental Health Center). The acknowledgments thank several colleagues, including a pharmacokinetic consultant and two investigators of the earlier phencyclidine work. No industry sponsor is named; the drug was a commercial preparation (Parke-Davis).

what_would_settle_it: A larger within-person study with a described and tested blind, measured plasma concentrations at every assessment, cognitive tests calibrated away from ceiling and floor (a word list long enough to show an immediate-recall effect, a card-sorting equivalent that can be repeated within person), pre-specified primary outcomes, and structured follow-up over weeks rather than an unstructured interview; with a second sample of people who use ketamine non-medically and of patients, so that tolerance and vulnerability can be separated from the drug effect.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the three test days)
domains.note: The three conditions were given in a randomized order, but no sequence generation or allocation concealment is described and no period or order effect is reported. Baseline scores did not differ between test days for most measures, which is reassuring; for plasma HVA they did (p. 208).

The interval between test days is not stated anywhere in the paper, so carryover cannot be judged from the report; ketamine's short half-life and the return of ratings to baseline within about 15 minutes after the infusion make pharmacological carryover unlikely, but learning effects across days are a real concern for the cognitive tests, and it is for exactly this reason that card sorting had to be analysed between participants.

'Double-blind' is asserted in the abstract only; no masking procedure, no rater independence and no blinding check are described. The 0.5 mg/kg condition caused blurred vision in 8 of 18 participants, nystagmus in about half of those and vomiting in 2, and participants had been told in advance what to expect, so neither participants nor raters are likely to have been blind in that condition. Most outcomes are clinician ratings and self-ratings.

One of 19 dropped out after one day and the analysed number falls to 14 to 17 for several measures. Two reasons are given (the vigilance test was added after four participants had entered; three fluency tests were discarded because they were not finished before the infusion ended, which could itself be an effect of the drug); for the CADSS (17), recall and cortisol (16), MHPG (15) and HVA (14) no reason is stated.

The hormone, metabolite and blood-pressure measures are objective (low on their own). The main outcomes are clinician ratings and self-ratings made in a condition that was probably recognizable, by raters whose blinding is not described; the recall and vigilance tasks were near ceiling, and the card-sorting version is an unpublished in-house one.

No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome; about 39 outcome measures plus item-level and correlation analyses with no correction across measures; some analyses (the peak-change analysis of drowsiness) appear only after a non-significant overall test. Against this, null results are reported for MMSE, MHPG, pulse, anger and sadness, and for the memory-symptom correlations.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The within-person design with a saline day in the same people, the randomized order and the placebo-correction of each change make the acute symptom and dissociation findings internally strong, and they have since been reproduced. The overall judgment is set by the blinding: the paper claims a double blind in its abstract while describing no masking in its methods, and the high-dose condition produced visible signs (blurred vision, nystagmus, vomiting) in a study whose main outcomes are clinician ratings and self-ratings. The source can be cited for what 40-minute intravenous infusions of 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg did in 18 screened healthy volunteers during and shortly after the session: the size and time course of the rise in psychotic-like, dissociative and perceptual-alteration ratings, the fall in delayed three-word recall and in verbal fluency, the absence of MMSE change, the hormone and metabolite changes and the modest blood-pressure rise. It cannot be cited for effects after the session, for any plasma concentration (none were measured), for the card-sorting effect as a within-person drug effect, for the sparing of immediate recall as a general finding, or for the safety of ketamine administration.

key_findings.finding: BPRS four key positive symptoms (conceptual disorganization, hallucinatory behavior, suspiciousness, unusual thought content) rose with dose in 18 healthy volunteers: dose F2,34=72.0, time F4,68=19.3, dose x time F8,136=22.9, all P=.0001. Placebo and 0.1 mg/kg produced no significant change from baseline; at 0.5 mg/kg the rise from baseline was significant at 10 minutes (t5,136=9.4) and 80 minutes (t5,136=12.8), P<.01, and remained significant after adjusting for the placebo day. Scores returned to baseline generally within 15 minutes of the end of the infusion.
key_findings.locator: Results > BPRS scores > Positive symptoms of schizophrenia, 1st paragraph; Figure 1, left panel
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Figure 1 (left panel), whose values are not printed: the 0.5 mg/kg mean rises from about 4.0 at baseline to about 8.0 at 10 minutes and about 9.4 at 80 minutes on a four-item cluster score whose minimum is 4, so the peak is about 5.4 points above the floor.

key_findings.finding: BPRS three key negative symptoms (blunted affect, emotional withdrawal, motor retardation) also rose with dose: dose F2,34=34.6, time F4,68=28.0, dose x time F8,136=18.0, all P=.0001. At 0.1 mg/kg the increase was significant only at 80 minutes (t5,136=2.56, P<.05); at 0.5 mg/kg at 10 minutes (t5,136=9.1) and 80 minutes (t5,136=12.6), P<.01, still significant after adjusting for placebo.
key_findings.locator: Results > BPRS scores > Negative symptoms of schizophrenia (p. 203, right column, continuing on p. 204); Figure 1, right panel (p. 203)

key_findings.finding: Dissociative symptoms (CADSS total, n=17) rose with dose: dose F2,32=65.0, time F3,48=46.8, dose x time F6,96=46.0, all P=.0001. Placebo produced no increase at any time point; at 0.1 mg/kg the increase at 80 minutes was not significant (t4,96=2.56, P<.1); at 0.5 mg/kg the increases at 10 minutes (t4,96=9.4) and 80 minutes (t4,96=18.8) were significant, P<.01, and remained so after adjusting for the placebo day. All five author-defined subscales (body perception, environmental perception, feelings of unreality, memory impairment, time perception) showed significant dose x time interactions (F6,96 from 17.6 to 30.0, P=.0001).
key_findings.locator: Results > Perceptual alterations > Clinician-Administered Dissociative States Scale, 1st paragraph and the following paragraph on the subscales
key_findings.note: The number analysed for the CADSS is given as 17 in the text and as 18 in the Figure 2 legend (see reporting issues). Editors' reading of Figure 2 (right panel, p. 204), whose values are not printed: the 0.5 mg/kg mean rises from about 0 at baseline to about 14 at 10 minutes and about 27 at 80 minutes.

key_findings.finding: Self-rated perceptual alterations (Perceptual Aberration Scale, n=18) rose with dose: dose F2,34=35.4, time F3,51=26.7, dose x time F6,102=20.0, all P=.0001; significant increases from baseline at 0.5 mg/kg at 10 minutes (t4,102=12.9) and 80 minutes (t4,102=18.7), P<.01, and after placebo adjustment. Peak increases on the clinician-rated CADSS and the self-rated Perceptual Aberration Scale on the 0.5 mg/kg day were not significantly correlated with each other.
key_findings.locator: Results > Perceptual alterations > Perceptual Aberration Subscale of the Wisconsin Psychosis Proneness Questionnaire, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The two BPRS factor scores also rose at the high dose (n=18). Activation: dose F2,34=11.8, time F4,68=10.1, dose x time F8,136=6.1, all P=.0001; the score rose from 3.2 (SEM 0.1) at baseline to 3.9 (0.2) at 10 minutes (t5,136=3.4) and 4.7 (0.5) at 80 minutes (t5,136=7.3), P<.01, and remained significant after placebo adjustment. Hostility-suspiciousness: dose F2,34=6.7 (P=.004), time F4,68=5.1 (P=.001), dose x time F8,136=6.1 (P=.0001), with a rise at the 80-minute time point only.
key_findings.locator: Results > BPRS activation factor score and > BPRS hostility-suspiciousness factor score
key_findings.note: The hostility-suspiciousness paragraph prints the activation means (3.2, SEM 0.1 and 4.7, SEM 0.5) and the word activation in place of hostility, and both factors are given the same interaction statistic F8,136=6.1, so the hostility-suspiciousness means cannot be read from the paper (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Global cognition on the MMSE (n=18) did not change significantly: dose x time F8,136=1.4, P=.2; peak decreases from baseline were 0.7 (SEM 0.4) points on placebo, 0.2 (0.1) at 0.1 mg/kg and 0.3 (0.2) at 0.5 mg/kg, dose effect F2,34=1.6, P=.2.
key_findings.locator: Results > Mini-Mental State Examination, only paragraph

key_findings.finding: Word recall (n=16) showed an interaction of dose, time and delay (F16,240=2.7, P=.0006). There was no dose x time interaction for immediate recall (F8,120=0.0, not significant), a non-significant trend for recall after distraction (F8,120=1.7, P=.1) and a significant interaction for 10-minute delayed recall (F8,120=3.4, P=.002), with a significant fall at 0.5 mg/kg.
key_findings.locator: Results > Memory (p. 206, right column, continuing on p. 207); Figure 4 (p. 207)
key_findings.note: Only three words were presented at each time point and immediate recall sat at or near 3 on every day (Figure 4, top panel, p. 207), so the task could not show a fall in immediate recall; the delayed-recall curve drops to about 1.2 words at the 10-minute time point on the 0.5 mg/kg day (Figure 4, bottom panel). The decrease from baseline is marked significant at that one time point only.

key_findings.finding: On the 0.5 mg/kg day the fall in delayed recall was not significantly correlated with the rise in positive symptoms (r=.2), negative symptoms (r=.07) or CADSS score (r=.2); n=16.
key_findings.locator: Results > Memory, last paragraph (p. 207, left column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: with n=16 a correlation of 0.2 has a 95% interval of about -0.33 to 0.63 (Fisher z), so these null results cannot show that the memory and symptom effects are independent. Signs are not printed, so even the direction of these three correlations is uncertain (reporting issue 2); the paper's statement that the memory effect is separate from the symptom effects rests on them.

key_findings.finding: Letter fluency (n=15) fell with dose: 16.1 (SEM 1.3) words on placebo, 15.1 (1.2) at 0.1 mg/kg and 12.9 (1.3) at 0.5 mg/kg; dose effect F2,28=4.4, P=.02; high dose against placebo F1=8.4, P=.007; low against high dose F1=3.8, P=.06.
key_findings.locator: Results > Measures of frontal lobe function > Verbal Fluency, only paragraph; Figure 3, left panel
key_findings.note: Three of the 18 participants' fluency tests were excluded because they were not finished before the infusion ended (p. 201). Individual values in Figure 3 (left) scatter from about 4 to 19 words on the 0.5 mg/kg day and from about 6 to 23 on placebo, with lines crossing in both directions.

key_findings.finding: Vigilance (continuous performance test, n=14) changed slightly and only at the high dose: targets correctly identified 29.7 (SEM 0.1) on placebo, 29.6 (0.2) at 0.1 mg/kg and 28.5 (0.4) at 0.5 mg/kg (F2,26=8.6, P=.001); omission errors 0.3 (0.1), 0.4 (0.2) and 1.5 (0.4) (F2,26=8.6, P=.001); commission errors 0.1 (0.1), 0.2 (0.2) and 0.6 (0.3) (F2,26=4.3, P=.03); reaction time did not change (0.48, 0.46 and 0.51 seconds; F2,24=1.8, P=.2).
key_findings.locator: Results > Measures of frontal lobe function > Vigilance (p. 205, right column, continuing on p. 206)
key_findings.note: The task was near its ceiling (29.7 of 30 correct on placebo), so the absolute change is about one target and about one extra omission.

key_findings.finding: On the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, compared between participants on their first test day only (placebo n=6, 0.1 mg/kg n=5, 0.5 mg/kg n=8), perseverative errors were 6.5 (SEM 0.8), 16.8 (7.9) and 31.9 (7.0); dose effect F2,16=4.6, P=.03, with 0.5 mg/kg significantly above placebo by the Student-Newman-Keuls test. Trials to the first category 13.5 (1.9), 14.6 (2.5) and 35.1 (7.8), F2,16=4.6, P=.03; total errors 12.8 (2.2), 25.6 (10.0) and 53.4 (8.4), F2,16=8.0, P=.004. Percent perseverative error did not differ (54%, 62%, 58%; F2,16=0.7, not significant), the number of correct items did not differ (70.8, 68.8, 65.6; F2,16=0.4, P=.7), losses of set did not differ (F2,16=2.0, P=.2), and all participants completed all six categories.
key_findings.locator: Results > Measures of frontal lobe function > Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, only paragraph; Figure 3, right panel
key_findings.note: This is a between-participant comparison of 6, 5 and 8 people with no baseline, not a within-person drug effect; editors' calculation from the SEMs gives SDs of about 2.0 (placebo), 17.7 (0.1 mg/kg) and 19.8 (0.5 mg/kg), and Figure 3 (right) shows one person at 0.1 mg/kg with about 48 errors and one at 0.5 mg/kg with about 75, against a placebo range of about 2 to 12.

key_findings.finding: Among the 19 first-day card-sorting participants, perseverative errors correlated with the peak rise in three key negative symptoms (r=.5, P=.05) and with the peak CADSS rise (r=.6, P=.008); correlations with the four key positive symptoms (r=.5, P<.06) and with the Perceptual Aberration Scale (r=.4, P=.06) were not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results > Measures of frontal lobe function > Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, paragraph beginning 'Since the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test cannot be repeated' (right column)
key_findings.note: Correlations across people who received different doses, so dose alone can produce them; the printed P values do not match two-sided tests on n=19 (editors' calculation: r=.5 gives P=.029, r=.6 gives P=.007, r=.4 gives P=.09), and the degrees of freedom are not printed.

key_findings.finding: Mood ratings (0 to 100 mm, n=18): the feeling of being high rose at 0.5 mg/kg at 10 minutes (t4,102=6.8) and 80 minutes (t4,102=5.1), P<.01; after placebo adjustment only the 10-minute point remained significant. Anxiety showed a biphasic pattern: at 0.5 mg/kg anxiety fell from baseline by 80 minutes (t4,102=5.5, P<.01) but, against the fall on the placebo day, it was significantly raised 10 minutes into the infusion (t3,102=4.7, P<.01); the fall in anxiety at 0.1 mg/kg lost significance once the placebo-day fall was taken into account. Anger, drowsiness and sadness showed no significant drug x time effects, but a separate analysis of peak increases showed a dose-related rise in drowsiness (6.2, SEM 4.3 mm on placebo; 15.5, 4.4 at 0.1 mg/kg; 22.9, 6.9 at 0.5 mg/kg; F2,34=4.3, P=.02).
key_findings.locator: Results > Visual analog scales of mood states > Anxiety and High (right column); Figure 5 (p. 208)

key_findings.finding: Plasma cortisol (n=16) rose with dose: dose F2,30=10.6 (P=.0003), time F4,60=4.1 (P=.005), dose x time F8,120=10.1 (P=.0001); against placebo, 0.5 mg/kg raised cortisol significantly (P<.01) at 40, 80 and 100 minutes. Prolactin (n=18) rose at 0.5 mg/kg at 40 minutes (t5,136=2.49, P<.05), still significant after placebo adjustment (dose F2,34=4.9, P=.01; dose x time F8,136=3.7, P=.0007). At 0.5 mg/kg the usual test-day fall in plasma HVA was blunted (peak change -0.9, SEM 0.4 ng/mL on placebo; -1.2, 0.6 at 0.1 mg/kg; +0.3, 0.6 at 0.5 mg/kg; placebo against high dose t13=2.4, P=.03), and MHPG did not change (dose x time F8,112=1.1, P=.4).
key_findings.locator: Results > Neuroendocrine indexes > Homovanillic acid, Cortisol and Prolactin; Figure 6 (p. 209)
key_findings.note: The text gives n=16 for cortisol while the Figure 6 legend gives n=18 (see reporting issues). The HVA effect is uncertain: baseline HVA was already lower on the 0.5 mg/kg day (10.3 against 14.7 ng/mL on placebo), and after covarying for baseline the dose effect was no longer significant.

key_findings.finding: Blood pressure rose modestly with dose: systolic drug x time F12,204=2.2 (P=.01), with peak increases from baseline of 11.3 (SEM 1.9) mm Hg on placebo, 13.2 (1.9) at 0.1 mg/kg and 18.6 (2.6) at 0.5 mg/kg (dose effect F2,34=2.9, P=.07); diastolic drug x time F12,204=3.6 (P=.0001), peak increases 5.9 (1.3), 6.9 (0.9) and 12.5 (2.2) mm Hg (F2,34=4.7, P=.02). Resting pulse showed no significant drug x time interaction (F12,204=1.1, P=.3).
key_findings.locator: Results > Blood pressure and pulse, only paragraph
key_findings.note: The placebo day itself showed a peak systolic rise of 11.3 mm Hg, so the drug-attributable part is about 7 mm Hg systolic and about 7 mm Hg diastolic (editors' calculation from peak changes that are not time-matched); the authors call the systolic finding loosely supported.

key_findings.finding: Other acute effects on the 0.5 mg/kg day: 8 of 18 participants (44%, 4 men and 4 women) reported blurred vision, about half of them with horizontal nystagmus, and 2 women vomited; both had blurred vision and nystagmus at the time. At follow-up interview no participant reported lingering or recurrent effects such as nightmares, flashbacks or perceptual alterations after a test day.
key_findings.note: Follow-up was a contact on the day after the 0.5 mg/kg infusion and interviews on later test days (p. 201); no structured instrument or defined follow-up period is described, so the absence of later effects is weak evidence.

key_findings.finding: None of the pre-test measures of vulnerability to psychosis (the Bell Reality Testing Inventory, its subscales, or the Wisconsin Psychosis Proneness Scale) correlated significantly with the placebo-corrected peak rise in positive symptoms (r<.25).
key_findings.locator: Results > BPRS scores > Positive symptoms of schizophrenia, last paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: In a sample screened to exclude people scoring outside normal limits on those same scales, the restricted range makes a null correlation close to uninformative; the authors make this point themselves (p. 211).

key_findings.finding: The authors state that at these doses hallucinatory behavior was limited to illusory experiences in all sensory domains, that is distortions of real stimuli rather than hallucinations, and describe ideas of reference, paranoid content and formal thought disorder at the higher dose.
key_findings.locator: Results > BPRS scores > Positive symptoms of schizophrenia, 2nd-3rd paragraphs (p. 203); Comment, 1st-2nd paragraphs (p. 209)
key_findings.note: A clinical description, not a measured outcome: the four key positive symptom items include hallucinatory behavior but item-level means are not printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The number analysed for the CADSS is given as 17 in the text and as 18 in the Figure 2 legend; for cortisol it is 16 in the text and 18 in the Figure 6 legend. The denominators behind the other analyses (15 for MHPG, 14 for HVA, 16 for recall) are stated without explanation.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader cannot tell how many people contributed to the dissociation and cortisol findings, and the denominators of the within-person analyses are uncertain. The degrees of freedom are consistent with the text values (CADSS F2,32 implies 17 participants, cortisol F2,30 implies 16), so the figure legends appear to be wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: The study is called randomized, double-blind and placebo-controlled in the abstract, but the Methods describe only the randomized order; there is no description of masking, of who made the ratings, or of any blinding check, and no statement that the rater was unaware of the condition.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study's main outcomes are clinician ratings and self-ratings in a condition that produced visible signs in nearly half the participants, so the claim of a double blind cannot be checked and should not be repeated as a fact about the study.

reporting_issues.issue: Dunnett's t statistics are printed with two subscripts (for example t5,136=9.4, t4,96=18.8) whose first number corresponds to the number of means being compared rather than to any degrees of freedom; degrees of freedom for the correlations are not printed at all, and correlations are printed without signs.
reporting_issues.consequence: The post-hoc tests cannot be recomputed from what is printed, and the direction of each correlation has to be inferred from the surrounding text.

reporting_issues.issue: The card-sorting P values are inconsistent with the printed statistics in places: the correlation of perseverative errors with negative symptoms is given as r=.5, P=.05 and with positive symptoms as r=.5, P<.06, the same correlation coefficient with two different P values, and r=.4 is reported with P=.06 while r=.5 is reported with P=.05.
reporting_issues.consequence: At n=19 a two-sided test gives P=.029 for r=.5 and P=.09 for r=.4 (editors' calculation), so neither the printed values nor the significance labels can be reproduced; these correlations should not be cited as evidence that card-sorting performance tracks symptoms.

reporting_issues.issue: The BPRS activation and hostility-suspiciousness sections print the same sentence about what did not change ('Neither placebo nor ketamine hydrochloride, 0.1 mg/kg, produced significant increases in activation from baseline') and the same means (3.2 at baseline, 4.7 at 80 minutes) under both headings, and the hostility paragraph reports increases in activation scores rather than in hostility-suspiciousness scores.
reporting_issues.consequence: The hostility-suspiciousness result as printed appears to be a copy of the activation result; the factor's own means cannot be read from the paper, so only the F statistics for that factor can be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's statement that ketamine 'preferentially disrupted delayed word recall, sparing immediate recall and postdistraction recall' rests on a task of three words at which immediate recall was at or near the maximum on all three days.
reporting_issues.consequence: A ceiling effect cannot be distinguished from a spared function. The Discussion concedes the point and cites a study with 24 words in which immediate recall was affected (p. 210); a claim of selective sparing of immediate recall must not rest on this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The sexes of the 18 completers are not stated, and the completer count itself is internally inconsistent: the sample sentence says that twelve men and seven women (19 people) completed the testing, while the next sentence says one withdrew after a first test day and the analyses use 18. The sample is described as 12 men and 7 women and one man dropped out, so the completers were presumably 11 men and 7 women, but the paper reports sex only in the dropped-out participant's case and says that data were collapsed across sexes because sex did not appear to influence responses, without showing any test.
reporting_issues.consequence: The composition of the analysed sample and the basis for pooling the sexes are both unverifiable; the sample is too small to detect a sex difference in any case.

reporting_issues.issue: The dose on the first test day was not balanced: 6 participants had placebo, 5 had 0.1 mg/kg and 8 had 0.5 mg/kg, and this is also the whole of the card-sorting comparison; the three first-day groups are not compared on age, sex or any baseline measure.
reporting_issues.consequence: The card-sorting dose effect is a comparison of three small unmatched groups, and pre-existing differences cannot be excluded; the within-person design does not protect this analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: Plasma ketamine concentrations were not measured; the paper's concentrations are predictions from published parameters fitted to constant-infusion equations.
reporting_issues.consequence: No finding of this study can be anchored to a measured blood level, and the predicted ranges (0.025 to 0.05 mg/L and 0.1 to 0.25 mg/L) should be described as predicted, not measured, wherever they are cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The time line of the ratings is not what it appears: the 80-minute rating was made 40 minutes after the infusion ended, but each rating covered the period since the previous one, so the 80-minute score reflects the last 30 minutes of the infusion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Peak symptom scores plotted at 80 minutes in Figures 1, 2, 5 and 6 are effects during the infusion, not after it; a claim about the duration of effect must use the authors' statement that scores returned to baseline generally within about 15 minutes of the end of the infusion rather than the figure's x-axis.
